 Louisiana Woman Convicted of Fraud, Obstruction, and Money Laundering in $17 Million Tax Refund Scheme 
 Office of U.S. Attorney | Western District of Louisiana 
 Nov 19, 2026 
 6 hrs ago

 ALEXANDRIA/ LAFAYETTE/ SHREVEPORT – On November 17, 2026, a federal jury convicted Jane Frances Pierce , 64, of Boyce, of mail fraud, filing false tax returns, corruptly interfering with an IRS investigation, and money laundering. 
 “Jane Pierce filed false tax returns through a purported trust she controlled and used those filings to fraudulently claim nearly $10 million in refunds from the IRS,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division. “After obtaining more than $1 million in taxpayer funds, Pierce used the money for personal expenses and then tried to obstruct the IRS’s recovery efforts through additional false filings, a fake check, and money laundering. Today’s conviction makes clear that the Fraud Division will hold accountable those who steal from the American people and attempt to hide or obstruct their crimes.”
 “Tax fraudsters steal not just from the United States government but also from every person who works hard, pays their taxes, and trusts that everyone else is doing the same,” said U.S. Attorney Zachary A. Keller. “When that trust is undermined through theft by people like Ms. Pierce, citizens lose trust in the systems that serve and protect our communities and that they pay for with their hard-earned tax dollars. The people of Western Louisiana deserve honesty and accountability, and we will continue working with our law enforcement partners to hold those offenders accountable for their actions.”
 “This conviction sends a powerful message to those who believe they can exploit our nation’s tax system for personal financial gain,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Maisha Horton, of IRS Criminal Investigation’s Atlanta Field Office. “IRS Criminal Investigation will investigate, uncover your schemes, and hold you accountable. I commend the outstanding work and unwavering determination of our IRS-CI special agents, whose investigative efforts were instrumental in securing this conviction, and thank the U.S. Attorney’s Office for its vigorous prosecution of this case. Together, we are sending an unmistakable message that stealing from the American taxpayer will have serious consequences.”
 According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Pierce filed false tax returns on behalf of a purported trust she controlled, fraudulently claiming a total of almost $10 million in refunds. Pierce obtained more than $1 million from the IRS and used the funds for personal expenses, including purchasing a house and paying her relatives’ mortgages. When the IRS attempted to recover the refunds she fraudulently obtained, Pierce obstructed the agency’s efforts by filing a false amended tax return, mailing the IRS a fake check, filing a false court document and laundering the remaining profits. Separately, Pierce filed a false tax return on behalf of a purported estate that she controlled claiming more than $7 million in refunds.
 After deliberating for approximately 40 minutes, the jury returned guilty verdicts on all counts. Following the verdict, the Court ordered Pierce to be held in custody pending sentencing. Pierce is scheduled to be sentenced on February 16. She faces maximum penalties of twenty years in federal prison for mail fraud, ten years in prison for each money laundering charge and three years in prison for the false tax return and corrupt interference charges. Pierce also faces a period of supervised release, restitution and monetary penalties. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. sentencing guidelines and other statutory factors.
 Assistant Attorney General Colin McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division and U.S. Attorney Zachary A. Keller of the Western District of Louisiana made the announcement.
 IRS Criminal Investigation investigated the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Thomas Johnson for the Western District of Louisiana and Trial Attorney Hayter L. Whitman of the Fraud Division’s Tax Section prosecuted the case, with assistance from Legal Assistant Tanya Broussard.
 On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the National Fraud Enforcement Division (Fraud Division). The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste and abuse within Federal benefit programs.
